# USS North Dakota (SSN 784) Changes Homeport to Pearl Harbor

By Lt.j.g. Samantha Prewitt, Commander, Submarine Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet Public Affairs

 JOINT BASE PEARL HARBOR-HICKAM, Hawaii–
Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USS North Dakota (SSN 784) arrived at its new home port of Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, Nov. 13, 2026. North Dakota completed an Extended Drydocking Selected Restricted Availability at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, in Kittery, Maine, before joining Submarine Squadron 1 as its sixth Virginia-class fast-attack submarine.

"The crew of North Dakota is excited to call Pearl Harbor our new home," said U.S. Navy Cmdr. Christopher Marolt, commanding officer, North Dakota. "Our Sailors have put forth herculean efforts to get through the shortest availability in Portsmouth Naval Shipyard history, all while managing a homeport change to a new submarine homeport. We are ready to integrate with Submarine Squadron 1 and reunite with our families.”

Following North Dakota's arrival to Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, the submarine’s crew earned the Retention Excellence award in 2024 and the Commander, Submarine Force Atlantic Battle Efficiency (“Battle E”) award in 2024 and 2025, recognizing the crew's superior readiness, performance, and efficiency.

"It is an honor to welcome the Sailors and families of North Dakota to Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam as the newest addition to the waterfront,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Christopher Hedrick, commodore, Submarine Squadron 1. "It is the dedication of this crew that brings this boat to life. We are proud to have you on the team, supporting our strategic advantage in the Pacific."

North Dakota, a Virginia-class fast-attack submarine, was commissioned Oct. 25, 2014, and is the second U.S. warship commissioned under the name North Dakota, the first being World War I-era battleship USS North Dakota (BB-29).

"Saying farewell to Portsmouth, New Hampshire, is bittersweet, as the community there has supported us tremendously throughout our maintenance and preparation period," said Marolt. "However, bringing a battle-tested, back-to-back Battle 'E' crew into the Pacific Fleet theater is an incredible honor. We carry the proud heritage of our namesake and our recent successes with us as we stand ready to project power and support our allies and partners in this vital region."

东盟保留对缅甸的限制，但为政治回归开辟道路
菲律宾总统小费迪南德·马科斯（右）和新加坡总理黄循财周日出席在马尼拉举行的东盟领导人交流会。 |泳池 / 法新社-JIJI

马尼拉 - 东南亚领导人周日表示，如果缅甸在解决五年危机的长期计划上取得进展，他们可能会考虑逐步恢复缅甸在该地区集团的全面政治代表权。
东南亚国家联盟 11 个成员国的领导人在马尼拉峰会上同意维持目前将缅甸排除在东盟峰会和外长会议上的全面政治代表权的政策。
但他们表示，如果缅甸在欧盟提出的计划（即五点共识或5PC）上取得“持续和具体”进展，他们同意通过“分阶段和基于进展”的方式进行“有针对性的接触”。
值得注意的是，该集团似乎还支持其成员国与缅甸进行双边接触。
近几个月来，泰国和其他几个东盟成员国加强了与缅甸的接触，给东盟带来了新的压力，要求其放宽对缅甸军方支持的领导人参加高级别会议的禁令。
领导人在峰会上通过的一项联合决定中表示：“如果缅甸在落实五项原则方面取得持续和具体进展，东盟可能会考虑逐步恢复缅甸的全面政治代表性。”
他们表示：“我们还鼓励东盟各成员国与所有相关利益攸关方进行建设性接触，并与东盟主席协商，推动 5PC 的实施取得实质性进展。”
2021 年缅甸军方夺取政权后不久，东盟就通过了五点共识，呼吁立即停止当地暴力，并在各方之间启动建设性对话。它提供东盟调解和人道主义援助。
缅甸军队支持的政府希望与东盟实现关系正常化。自从军方推翻诺贝尔和平奖获得者昂山素季的民选政府以来，该国一直处于动荡之中，引发了一场内战，联合国估计这场内战已造成 10 万人死亡，超过 350 万人流离失所。
政变领导人、现任总统敏昂莱的军队得到了中国、印度和俄罗斯的支持。近几个月来，他的政府获得了越来越多的国际认可，包括在唐纳德·特朗普总统的政府扭转多年的孤立状态时与美国官员进行秘密会谈。

Manila – Southeast Asian leaders said on Sunday they may ​consider gradually restoring Myanmar’s full political representation in the regional bloc, if ‌the country makes ‌progress on their longstanding plan to resolve its five-year-old crisis.
Leaders ​of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations agreed at a summit in Manila to maintain their policy of excluding Myanmar from full political representation at ASEAN summits ⁠and foreign ministers’ meetings for now.
But they said they had agreed to pursue a “calibrated engagement” ⁠through a “phased and progress-based” approach, if Myanmar makes “sustained and concrete” progress on the bloc’s proposed plan, known as the five-point consensus, or 5PC.
And ​in a notable step, the bloc ⁠also appeared to endorse bilateral outreach to Myanmar among its member countries.
Thailand and several other ASEAN members have stepped ⁠up engagement with Myanmar ​in recent months, creating new pressureon the bloc to ease ​its ban on Myanmar’s military-backed leaders attending its high-level meetings.
“Subject to ​sustained and ‌concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the leaders said in a joint decision adopted at the summit.
“We also encourage efforts by individual ASEAN ‌Member States through constructive engagement with all relevant stakeholders, in consultation with the ASEAN Chair, to advance substantive progress in the implementation of the 5PC,” they said.
ASEAN’s five-point consensus, adopted soon after the military seized power in Myanmar in 2021, calls for an immediate end ​to ​violence there and for the launch of constructive dialogue among ​all parties. It offers ASEAN mediation and humanitarian assistance.
Myanmar’s army-backed government wants to normalise ⁠ties with ASEAN. The country has been in turmoil since the military ousted Nobel Peace Prize winner Aung San Suu Kyi’s elected government, triggering a civil war that the U.N. estimates has killed 100,000 people and displaced more than ​3.5 million.
Coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing’s military has received support from China, India and Russia. His administration has gained increasing international recognition in recent months, including secret talks with U.S. officials as President Donald Trump’s administration reverses years of isolation.

CTI 视频片段的屏幕截图显示，2025 年 5 月，一名名为 Alice Huang 的女性在台北与时任 Nvidia 首席执行官 Jensen Huang 共进晚餐后离开餐厅。 CTI / 来自路透社

新加坡——总部位于新加坡的数据中心公司 Megaspeed International 因涉嫌将 Nvidia 芯片运往中国而受到审查，该公司周日表示，涉嫌间谍的 Alice Huang 已于一年多前离开该公司。
Megaspeed 涉嫌通过为其东南亚数据中心购买 Nvidia 芯片并将其运往中国，帮助中国公司绕过美国出口管制。
该公司前董事黄爱丽 (Alice Huang) 被美国媒体认定为所谓的中国情报人员，她与英伟达联合创始人黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 有关系，黄仁勋于周四辞去了这家科技巨头首席执行官的职务。
该公司表示：“Alice Huang 女士于 2025 年 8 月 30 日正式离开 Megaspeed，目前在该公司没有任何职位。”
“Megaspeed不对黄女士的个人和私人事务发表评论。”
Alice Huang 和 Jensen Huang 没有血缘关系。北京否认了间谍指控。
黄仁勋在 11 月 8 日致 Nvidia 员工的一封信中承认了婚外情，但没有透露涉案女性的姓名。几天后他辞职了。
英伟达董事会已表示将调查此事，三位美国国会委员会主席已要求黄仁勋参加 11 月 18 日举行的闭门简报会。
Megaspeed 表示，它“开展合法合法的业务”，并且知道媒体报道“包含有关我们业务、供应链和全球运营的断言，但这些断言没有可验证的证据支持”。
该科技集团还表示，已聘请外部法律顾问，对其在美国出口管制法下的合规义务进行“彻底的内部调查”，该法限制了一些先进芯片向中国的转移。
新加坡当局表示，包含先进人工智能芯片的服务器正在出口到马来西亚，并涉嫌运往其他目的地，这与新加坡的声明相反。
新加坡警方表示，对 Megaspeed 的调查“正在进行中”。
当局还表示，由于爱丽丝·黄 (Alice Huang) 在对 Megaspeed 的调查中提供了不准确的信息，他们于二月份禁止她重新进入新加坡。
然而，她并未因间谍活动而受到调查。

Singapore – Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed International, under scrutiny for allegedly steering Nvidia chips to China, said on Sunday that suspected spy Alice Huang had left the firm more than a year ago.
Megaspeed is suspected of helping Chinese firms get around U.S. export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia and routing them to China.
Its former director, Alice Huang, has been identified in U.S. media as an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who had a relationship with Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who resigned as the tech giant’s chief executive on Thursday.
“Ms Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” the firm said.
“Megaspeed does not comment on Ms Huang’s personal and private matters.”
Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are not related. Beijing has denied the spying allegations.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a Nov. 8 letter to Nvidia employees that did not name the woman involved. He resigned days later.
Nvidia’s board has said it will investigate the matter, and three U.S. Congress committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to attend a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18.
Megaspeed said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business“, and that it was aware of media reports “containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence“.
The tech group also said it has retained an external legal counsel “to conduct a thorough internal investigation” of its compliance obligations under U.S. export control laws, which limit the transfer of some advanced chips to China.
Singapore authorities said servers containing advanced AI chips were being exported to Malaysia and were suspected of being delivered to other destinations, contrary to declarations made in the city-state.
Investigations into Megaspeed “are ongoing“, Singapore’s police force has said.
Authorities also said they had barred Alice Huang in February from re-entering the city-state after she provided inaccurate information during a probe into Megaspeed.
She was not, however, investigated for espionage.

As the Pentagon finalizes its review of U.S. force posture in Europe, one relatively small commitment deserves protection from the budget axe: the roughly 600 American troops serving in NATO’s Kosovo Force. They barely register in a debate about brigades and billion-dollar line items, but they keep a hard-won peace in the Balkans, and pulling them out would save almost nothing while handing Moscow a cheap strategic win. KFOR was deployed in June 1999 under NATO command, after the alliance bombed Yugoslavia to stop the violence perpetrated by Slobodan Milosevic’s Serbian forces against ethnic Albanians. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, but Serbia, backed by Russia and China, still refuses to recognize it. The Europe posture review is a legitimate exercise. After years of urging European allies to shoulder more of their own conventional defense, the Trump administration is right to ask hard questions about where American forces add unique value and where Europe can step up given suitable time to develop their capabilities and capacities. But KFOR is a mission in which the American role is not easily replaced, because it is as much political as military, and where a wrong call risks instability on Europe’s southeastern flank. Start with the threat. Even while absorbing heavy losses in Ukraine, Vladimir Putin has not given up on destabilizing Europe. The Balkans, Europe’s soft underbelly, are a favored arena: cheap to stir, a place to distract Western attention from Ukraine. Moscow has long used Serbia as a lever against Kosovo’s stability. In 2017, a Russian-made train was sent toward northern Kosovo, a rolling provocation that bore the slogan “Kosovo is Serbia.” Russia runs a so-called humanitarian center near Kosovo that is suspected of serving as a Russian intelligence station. Close Serbian-Russian intelligence ties give Moscow access to local nationalist forces prepared for provocations. In 2023, an armed attack on Kosovo police in the north, which Pristina blamed on Serbian-backed militants, heightened fears that Russian-aligned actors were exploiting the tension; earlier that year, Russia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs warned that “a major explosive situation is brewing in the heart of Europe.” Tensions have repeatedly flared. In May 2023, clashes between Serb protesters and Kosovo police injured more than 90 NATO peacekeepers and prompted Serbia to raise its military alert level. That September, an attack in Banjska, where heavily armed Serb gunmen killed a Kosovo police officer and barricaded themselves in a monastery, showed how quickly a local flare-up can become a regional crisis. The danger has not passed. Serbian strongman Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in Serbia’s Oct. 25 parliamentary election, but Belgrade’s foreign-policy direction is uncertain and there are concerns that its views on Kosovo will not change. In October, Russia’s ambassador to the UN warned that the situation in Kosovo “remains persistently tense and is literally teetering on the brink.” Still, Kosovo and Serbia have remained at peace since 1999, in large part because of KFOR. In the words of a bipartisan group of U.S lawmakers, the force functions as “a political deterrent to those seeking to stoke ethnic violence.” An American drawdown from KFOR may embolden nationalist agendas in Kosovo and Serbia as well as separatist ambitions in Republika Srpska, the Serb-dominated region in nearby Bosnia. The American presence in KFOR is valued precisely because it is American. U.S. troops have anchored KFOR since its creation, and Washington currently leads Regional Command East, a position of real operational weight, not symbolism. The U.S. has traditionally provided the 600 or so American troops—often Army National Guardsmen—an economy-of-force mission with minimal cost or effect on the U.S. Army’s ability to execute missions elsewhere around the globe. The mission accounts for less than 1 percent of the total U.S. troops in Europe. KFOR’s value becomes plain when contrasted with Operation Althea in neighboring Bosnia. EUFOR, an EU-led force with roughly 1,500 troops, has struggled to respond decisively to repeated provocations by Republika Srpska leader Milorad Dodik, who’s backed by Moscow and Belgrade. EU ambassadors rejected Bosnian appeals to help enforce an arrest warrant against him in 2025, citing political risk. Dodik has openly mocked EUFOR’s patrols. Lacking an American anchor and a unified chain of command willing to act, EUFOR has too often had to manage crises rather than deterring them. KFOR, by contrast, has demonstrated it can surge forces when tested, providing genuine deterrence. After the 2023 Banjska incident, NATO increased its peacekeeping presence in Kosovo. Serbia drew down its border deployment, ending the crisis. The Pentagon is right to ask what the value of an American military presence is worth. For KFOR, the answer is plain: a few hundred U.S. troops are successfully maintaining a quarter-century-long peace that Russia would love to see unravel. Lawmakers from both parties already understand that. The Pentagon should, too, and keep KFOR intact. Mark Montgomery, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral, serves as a senior director at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ (FDD), where Ivana Stradner is a research fellow. ]]>

Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Posted Aug 14, 2026 by Martin Armstrong |
The Center for Strategic and International Studies conducted an extraordinary survey of 64 leading experts on China, Taiwan, and cross-Strait relations, including 28 former senior U.S. government officials, 23 former government policy and intelligence analysts, and 13 academics and think-tank experts. What their answers reveal is not that China is preparing to invade Taiwan tomorrow, as the neocons would like everyone to believe, but that Beijing remains willing to wait so long as nobody crosses the line of formal Taiwanese independence. Some 84% said Beijing is willing to wait for unification but will not accept the status quo permanently, while only 10% believed China seeks unification at the earliest opportunity. Not one of the 64 experts believed Beijing would ever accept an independent Taiwan.
This is precisely why Taiwan has become so dangerous. The West keeps portraying the conflict as if Xi Jinping wakes up every morning staring at a calendar trying to decide when to launch an amphibious invasion. Yet 83% of these experts said China did not plan to use significant kinetic force against Taiwan by 2027, and 80% said China’s enormous 2022 military exercises did not indicate Beijing had accelerated its timetable. Only 6% of respondents outside the former senior government group saw 2027 as a hard deadline, while not one former senior U.S. official did. The obsession with 2027 has nevertheless become extremely useful for the military establishment because every supposed deadline becomes another justification for weapons, deployments, bases, and spending.
The survey found that 44% believed Beijing has a hard deadline of 2049, the centennial of the People’s Republic, while 42% believed China could wait indefinitely provided unification remains possible. This is an important distinction because China thinks in terms of generations while Western politicians think in terms of the next election. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan if economic, political, and military pressure can gradually change the situation in its favor. Only 20% of those surveyed believed China even possessed a coherent roadmap for peaceful unification, which tells us this is not some perfectly scripted invasion plan sitting in Xi’s desk drawer.
Where the numbers become alarming is not an unprovoked invasion but what happens when politicians begin crossing China’s red lines. More than three-quarters of the experts, 77%, believed China would invade within six months if Taiwan formally declared independence. Among former senior U.S. officials, that number was 79%. Even some of those who did not expect an immediate invasion believed Beijing would respond with a blockade or enormous military exercises. This is why politicians encouraging Taiwan toward formal independence are playing with the lives of 23 million people. They can deliver all the speeches they want about democracy from Washington, London, or Brussels, but they will not be the civilians sitting underneath the missiles if their political experiment goes wrong.
Not one expert believed an explicit American commitment to defend Taiwan would cause China to invade immediately, but 64% believed Beijing would respond strongly enough to provoke a U.S.-China or China-Taiwan crisis, while another 31% expected a more limited negative response. Only two of the 64 experts believed formally committing America to Taiwan’s defense would actually deter China from using force because Beijing already assumes that the United States will intervene anyway.
A direct invasion is not even the most likely path toward conflict. Only 8% of the experts described an amphibious invasion within ten years as likely, while 63% called it possible and 27% unlikely. Force short of invasion received much higher probabilities, with 52% saying deliberate escalation such as a blockade was likely or very likely. An accidental military incident was considered even more dangerous, with 34% saying a collision or accident around the Taiwan Strait was likely and another 22% calling it very likely. When warships and aircraft from opposing nuclear powers continually operate around the same small body of water, war does not require some grand master plan. It requires one mistake followed by politicians who refuse to back down.
A later CSIS survey of American and Taiwanese experts reinforces that point. Roughly 90% of U.S. experts and 62% of Taiwanese experts believed China already possessed the capability to impose a law-enforcement-led quarantine that substantially reduces trade into Taiwan. Around 80% of American experts and 60% of Taiwanese experts believed Beijing could execute a PLA blockade, while Taiwanese experts were considerably more skeptical that China could successfully carry out an invasion. If Beijing wanted to coerce Taiwan during the following five years, experts considered a quarantine the most likely option. If China decided it wanted immediate unification, however, approximately 80% regarded a highly kinetic joint blockade as likely or very likely.
This is where the economic consequences become enormous because Taiwan does not need to be invaded for the world economy to be thrown into chaos. A quarantine or blockade would immediately threaten shipping, insurance, semiconductor supply chains, electronics, automobiles, communications equipment, and virtually every modern industry dependent upon advanced chips. The later CSIS survey found most American and Taiwanese experts did not believe Taiwan could withstand a Chinese blockade for longer than three months without substantial U.S. intervention. Washington would then face the decision nobody wants to discuss honestly: accept China’s blockade or attempt to break it militarily and risk direct war between two nuclear powers.
Taiwan is also the world’s semiconductor pressure point. The island’s importance to advanced chip manufacturing means a serious blockade would not remain a regional event. Factories thousands of miles away could discover that a conflict they thought had nothing to do with them suddenly prevents them from obtaining critical components. Markets would begin repricing the risk immediately, shipping premiums would explode, companies would scramble for inventory, and governments would discover once again how fragile global supply chains have become. This is why capital will react long before politicians formally declare that a war has begun.
What I find particularly revealing in the later CSIS survey is the difference between American confidence and Taiwanese confidence in Washington. An astonishing 96% of American experts were completely or moderately confident that the United States would intervene militarily if China invaded Taiwan during the following five years. Taiwanese experts were less confident in American intervention and considerably less confident that U.S. allies would join the fight. It is always easier for people thousands of miles away to be certain about somebody else’s war.
This is precisely why Taiwan remains one of the critical geopolitical pressure points as we move toward 2029. The danger is not simply that China arbitrarily decides to invade. The greater danger is escalation, miscalculation, political promises that cannot be withdrawn, and Western policymakers convincing themselves that every additional provocation somehow produces deterrence. China has made its position on formal independence perfectly clear, and even the experts inside the Western foreign-policy establishment overwhelmingly acknowledge that Beijing would react with force if that line were crossed.
If Taiwan declares formal independence, 77% of the experts surveyed believed China would invade within six months. That is not a statistic policymakers should treat as another war-game scenario. It is a warning about what happens when politicians deliberately remove the ambiguity that has helped keep the peace.

Office of the Spokesman Joint Statement on the G7 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Paris Media Note November 13, 2026 The following statement was released by the G7 Foreign Ministers of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom, the United States of America and the High Representative of the European Union. Begin Text: Joint declaration following the G7 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Paris on 9 and 10 November 2026 We, the G7 Foreign Ministers representing Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America, along with the High Representative of the European Union, met under the 2026 French G7 Presidency in Paris, on 9 and 10 November 2026. Ukraine We reaffirmed our unwavering support to Ukraine and its courageous people as they defend their territorial integrity, sovereignty, freedom, and independence. We stand in full solidarity with the Ukrainian population suffering from daily Russian attacks affecting residential buildings, civilian infrastructure, and cultural heritage, as well as malicious hybrid activities against Ukraine and other partners. We condemned the campaign of strikes carried out against civilian shipping in the Black Sea area, which have significant consequences on global food security, and strengthened our commitment to safeguarding food supply chains. We reiterated our support to ongoing U.S.-led efforts to facilitate peace through direct and serious negotiations. We reaffirmed the importance of securing a full, comprehensive, and reciprocal ceasefire. A reciprocal halt to attacks on all energy infrastructure and in the Black Sea to protect civilians, reduce disruption to energy, including heating, water and sanitation, and food supply and support greater stability in global markets is an important first step towards just and lasting peace. We reiterated that negotiations on the future security of Europe must include the Europeans. As we pledged during the G7 Summit in Évian, we took stock of progress on supplying Ukraine with air defense capabilities, systems and interceptors, long-range capabilities and licenses that will allow it to increase its military production and to exercise its inherent right of self-defense. We remain committed to continuing and strengthening our efforts in this direction. We acknowledged the need to address Ukraine’s pressing financing needs for 2027 and beyond in a coordinated way to support Ukraine. We condemned the provision of military assistance to Russia by North Korea and Iran, and the provision of weapons, military training and dual-use components by China, which enables the continuation of the war. We made clear our intention to continue to take action against these countries. Building on the consensus among our leaders in Évian, we discussed increasing pressure on Russia’s war economy, including through sanctions. We reaffirmed the commitment of our leaders to closely coordinate on sanctions against Russia. We reiterated our determination to focus on ships flying false flags or stateless ships, as well as structural enablers, such as insurers, oil traders, and intermediaries, to further disrupt and deter shadow fleet vessels used to circumvent sanctions. We reaffirmed our support to Ukraine’s energy security and resilience, and decided to step up our financial and material support to help the country get through the winter. We welcomed efforts to keep the repair of the Chornobyl New Safe Confinement high on the international agenda, as demonstrated by the donors’ conference organized in Paris on 9 November by France, EBRD, and Ukraine. We also welcomed the ongoing projects coordinated through the Tallinn Mechanism under Italy’s Chairpersonship to support Ukraine’s civilian cyber resilience. Middle East On Iran, we commended the work of the regional mediators and reiterated our support for all diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a lasting settlement that addresses international concerns over Iran’s nuclear program and contributes to regional security. We reiterated that Iran must never be allowed to develop or acquire a nuclear weapon. We urged Iran to stop its support for nonstate armed groups in the region. Absent a diplomatic solution, we committed to continuing our coordination to economically and politically constrain the Iranian regime’s ability to sow instability in the region and around the world. We strongly condemned Iran’s attacks against its neighbors and the disruption of international trade, energy security, and the global economy caused by the obstruction of transit passage through the Strait of Hormuz. We reaffirmed the importance of protecting civilians and civilian objects, and called on Iran to respect its international human rights and humanitarian law obligations. We called on Iran to cease its persistent attacks against civilian vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. We reaffirmed our commitment to the right of safe and free passage and our opposition to any tolls, fees, illegal costs, discriminations or any limitation imposed on maritime transit through the Strait. We underscored the importance of the defensive activities undertaken by U.S. Central Command in the Strait of Hormuz to demine the waterway and escort civilian vessels. We recognized that the multinational, independent, and defensive initiative led by France and the UK can play an important role in facilitating the resumption of maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz also by supporting the verification of the removal of all mines. We reaffirmed our commitment to fully implement the obligations under all relevant UN Security Council resolutions sanctions and related restrictive measures reinstated in September 2025 through the snapback mechanism under UN Security Council resolution 2231, and called on all UN Member States to do the same. We urged Iran to return to compliance with its international obligations, and in particular to resume full cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in order to restore transparency regarding the nature of its nuclear program. We also expressed grave concern over Iranian involvement in violent plots against many of our citizens and territories. We recognized the United Kingdom’s attribution of Iran’s involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford on 27 September. Iran should be in no doubt that we are united and remain committed to safeguarding our sovereignty. On Yemen, we condemned in the strongest terms the unacceptable continued strikes carried out by the Houthis in Yemen and against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, including those on civilians and civilian infrastructure. We called on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions and threats and refrain from any further escalation to enable a return to an inclusive political process. We expressed our solidarity with the Government of Yemen and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and reaffirmed their right to defend their security, sovereignty and territorial integrity in accordance with international law. We urged all actors, including Iran, to end their arming of and support for the Houthis, in violation of several United Nations Security Council resolutions. We expressed deep concern at the worsening humanitarian impact of the conflict and called for the protection of civilians and safe, unimpeded humanitarian access with the urgent opening of a humanitarian corridor in Taiz. We reiterated our call for the immediate and unconditional release of all humanitarian personnel, including the 70 UN staff who remain unjustly detained by the Houthis. We reaffirmed the importance of maritime safety and security in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. We shared the importance of continuing support to the Government of Yemen, including through capacity-building. We recognized the positive contribution of the EU maritime defensive operations EUNAVFOR ASPIDES and EUNAVFOR ATALANTA to restore maritime security and protect maritime shipping and the lives of seafarers in the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. On Lebanon, we stressed the need for all parties to fully respect the ceasefire and expressed support for implementation of the Trilateral Framework and of UN Security Council Resolution 1701. We reiterated that the disarmament of all non-state armed groups, foremost among them Hezbollah, remains essential to ensuring that all weapons are brought under the authority and control of the Lebanese state. We called on Lebanon and Israel to make progress implementing the pilot zones to allow for full and verifiable Hezbollah disarmament and Israeli redeployment as the Lebanese Armed Forces (LAF) deploy. We reiterated our support for the Lebanese authorities’ efforts to achieve the disarmament of all non-state armed groups and for Lebanese sovereignty and territorial integrity. As the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) is set to expire at the end of the year, we underscored the need for a robust, credible, and long-lasting security architecture in Lebanon in support of the LAF, in line with UN Security Council resolution 1701 and enabling further implementation of the Trilateral Framework. In calling for a strengthened LAF, we welcomed the establishment of the EU CSDP mission EU Support Mission in Lebanon (EUSM Lebanon). We called upon Lebanese actors to move forward in the adoption and implementation of financial reforms in view of agreeing on an IMF program. On Gaza, we remained committed to the swift implementation of UN Security Council Resolution 2803 and to accelerate humanitarian, recovery and reconstruction efforts aimed at fostering long-term stability. We unequivocally condemned the attacks committed by Hamas on the 7th of October, reiterating that Hamas can have no role in Gaza’s future and must decommission its weaponry. Israel must progressively withdraw from the Gaza Strip, under the conditions outlined in UN Security Council Resolution 2803. We stressed the urgent need for the safe, rapid, sustained, and unimpeded delivery of humanitarian assistance throughout Gaza and the opening of additional crossings, as well as the rehabilitation of humanitarian infrastructure and the protection of civilians. It is vital that all parties continue to engage constructively on the next steps outlined in the Comprehensive Plan, in pursuit of a political horizon for peaceful and prosperous coexistence, for the Israeli and Palestinian people, that advances Middle East peace and stability. We called for ending terrorist attacks and other actions which increase tensions and the risk of escalation in the West Bank. On Syria, we reaffirmed our strong support for a peaceful and inclusive political transition towards a united, sovereign and stable Syria, ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all Syrians. We stressed the importance of fully implementing the arrangements reached on the peaceful integration of Northeast Syria and reiterated our commitment to fighting terrorism. We expressed concern over the situation in Southern Syria, calling for the protection of civilians and respect for Syria’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. We also reaffirmed the importance of supporting Syria’s economic recovery and reconstruction to achieve lasting stability and to enhance regional connectivity. Indo-Pacific We emphasised the importance of a free and open Indo-Pacific region which is prosperous and secure, and that protects shared principles including sovereignty, territorial integrity, the rule of law, and the peaceful settlement of disputes. We reiterated our commitment to upholding freedom of navigation and overflight in the region and called on States to abide by their obligations under international law, as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). We expressed our serious concerns over the situation in the East China Sea and the South China Sea. We reaffirmed our strong opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo, particularly by force or coercion or any actions that raise tensions and risk escalation. We reiterated that the award rendered by the Arbitral Tribunal on 12 July 2016 is a significant milestone, which is final and legally binding upon the parties to the proceedings. We stressed the importance of maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait. In the context of China’s increasingly assertive activities in the waters east of Taiwan, which threaten regional stability, freedom of navigation and the safety of international shipping, we reaffirmed our opposition to any unilateral attempts to change the status quo, particularly by force or coercion, or the threat thereof. We encouraged the peaceful resolution of cross-Strait issues through constructive dialogue. We also expressed our support for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations. We strongly condemned North Korea’s unlawful nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs and reaffirmed our commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea, in accordance with all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions. We underlined that increased cooperation between Russia and North Korea has serious consequences for European and Indo-Pacific security. We urged North Korea to immediately cease all assistance and to withdraw its troops. We reaffirmed our concern regarding cryptocurrency thefts and cybercrimes committed by North Korea and expressed the need to respond to its unlawful overseas labor program. We urged North Korea to immediately resolve the issue of abductions. We remain deeply concerned by the deterioration of the human rights and humanitarian situation across Myanmar. We reiterated the need for the immediate de-escalation of violence, the unimpeded passage of humanitarian assistance, and a genuine and inclusive democratic process that reflects the will of the people of Myanmar. Sudan We were alarmed by the devastating consequences of the war on the Sudanese people and the growing risk of famine in parts of Darfur and Kordofan. Continued fighting, restrictions on humanitarian access and attacks, including by drones, affecting healthcare facilities, displacement camps and the infrastructure civilians rely on for food are putting lives at risk, which is being compounded by the impact of El Niño. A year after the atrocities in El Fasher, we unequivocally condemned all violations and abuses against civilians, including conflict-related sexual violence against women and girls. We called on all external actors to cease supplying or facilitating armed, logistical, and financial support to the belligerents and to use their influence to encourage the warring parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, lift restrictions on humanitarian access and support de-escalation, and avoid any action that could contribute to the conflict. We underscored that, beyond an immediate cease-fire, a peaceful and durable resolution of the conflict is essential to securing unity and long-term stability in Sudan. In line with the principles stated at the Sudan Ministerial Conference in Berlin in April this year, we reaffirmed that a credible Sudanese civilian-led, inclusive, and transparent political dialogue process that addresses historical grievances and respects Sudan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is critical to securing a lasting peace. We demanded the Rapid Support Forces and the Sudanese Armed Forces comply with international humanitarian law, engage in negotiations including with the Quad with a view to reaching a permanent ceasefire, and guarantee rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access. We reiterated our full support to the work of the Quintet aiming to facilitate such a dialogue, in a process that should run in parallel to and in close alignment with efforts to secure a ceasefire. We call on the wider international community to support these efforts. Horn of Africa We noted with great concern the worsening security situation in the Horn of Africa, specifically between Ethiopia and Eritrea, which bears the risk of regional escalation amid rising cross-border tensions. We underlined the serious consequences further escalation could have for regional stability, already dire humanitarian crises, security and international trade, including in the Red Sea. We called on all parties to exercise maximum restraint, pursue diplomatic solutions, and ensure safe and unhindered humanitarian access and the protection of civilians, especially women and children. We reaffirmed the importance of respecting the sovereignty, political independence and territorial integrity of all countries in the region. In particular, we supported efforts by the United Nations and the African Union to reduce tensions and to facilitate dialogue between the parties. Haiti We supported and welcomed the renewal of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF) mandate through March 2027, which aims to assist Haitian forces in restoring security and stability in Haiti. We also welcomed the renewal of the UN sanctions regime, which promotes accountability for individuals and entities who threaten peace, security, and stability in Haiti. We called for international support to strengthen the Haitian National Police and Haitian Armed Forces, uphold the rule of law, and combat impunity. We also called on all security actors operating in Haiti to prioritize the protection of Haitian civilians in all security operations. We stressed the importance of organizing democratic elections in Haiti and noted the postponement of the first round of elections to July 2027. Noting progress made by the government and the Provisional Electoral Council in their work to advance Haiti’s path to elected governance, we underlined the need to safeguard the credibility and integrity of the electoral process and underscored the responsibility of Haitian authorities to ensure their full and impartial implementation of the electoral decree. We called for concrete results that strengthen public confidence in the electoral process and contribute to a credible return to democratic governance. We noted with concerns regarding the participation of sanctioned individuals in the political process, which undermines accountability and public trust. The people of Haiti have a right to determine their future through credible democratic processes and leaders who serve the public interest with integrity. We remain deeply concerned by the ongoing humanitarian crisis, widespread violence, and reports of human rights violations in Haiti. We urged the international community to intensify financial contributions to the UN Trust Fund, recognizing that the success of the UN-mandated hybrid mission depends on sustained multilateral support to resource its operations. We urged critical international support for humanitarian assistance for Haiti, in order to address the multiple crises facing the people of Haiti. We also underscored the importance of laying the groundwork for Haiti’s economic recovery with the support of international financial institutions and other multilateral partners. We welcomed the World Bank’s Compact with the Haitian authorities as a common framework to assess Haitian-led reform efforts and strengthen accountability for results. We committed to working with diverse Haitian and international partners to promote greater coordination and complementarity of efforts. Cuba We expressed our concerns about the profound economic crisis and humanitarian needs facing the Cuban people, including shortages of food, fuel and medicines. We stressed the importance of improving humanitarian aid delivery mechanisms into and throughout Cuba in order to improve the welfare of the Cuban people. We called on the Cuban authorities to pursue and implement significant and meaningful political and economic reforms to advance prosperity, respect for human rights, and the legitimate aspirations of the Cuban people, and to take concrete steps towards multi-party democratic governance, press freedom, and freedom of expression and association. We also called on the Cuban authorities to release all individuals who have been arbitrarily detained. We encouraged constructive and inclusive dialogue in order to find a way out of the crisis. Venezuela We acknowledged the will of the people of Venezuela to turn the page on the country’s prolonged political and economic crisis. In this regard, we reaffirmed our full support for the ongoing reconciliation talks that bring together the interim government and the delegation representing the National Assembly elected in 2015 and which have already yielded measurable progress. We called on all parties to continue to engage in good faith on the path leading from the restoration of institutions and the rule of law to the holding of free and fair elections. We emphasised the particular importance of providing guarantees to all parties and civil society organizations to enable their participation in the democratic process. We called for the release of all political prisoners. We acknowledged that Venezuela’s economic recovery is inextricably linked to the political reconciliation process and encouraged investments and commercial deals that help build a more stable and prosperous future for the Venezuelan people. We also offered emergency humanitarian response and civil protection activities following the devastating twin earthquakes on June 24, 2026. UN reform and efficiency of humanitarian assistance Committed to making the UN more efficient and effective, accountable and impactful, we welcomed ongoing efforts under the UN80, as well as humanitarian reform initiatives, including the Humanitarian Reset. These latter initiatives aim to strengthen the humanitarian system through better coordination, mandate delineation, and consolidation of common services and critical enablers, while remaining fully open to all impartial humanitarian actors and in full compliance with international law and the UN Charter. We reiterated the importance of maintaining sustained momentum in driving forward reform at this critical juncture for the UN. We commended the work of the G7 working group on the efficiency of the humanitarian supply chain (LOG+7), which is one of the most strategic drivers to increase the impact of assistance in a context of a significant decrease in financing and worsening of crises. These efforts towards a more integrated supply chain, including the reinforcement of the existing humanitarian hubs and pooling of resources, will help reach a greater proportion of the population in need without budgetary changes, and thereby contributing to address growing humanitarian needs including food insecurity and malnutrition in all its forms. This work will continue within the framework of the Humanitarian Leadership Group on Supply Chain led by the European Union and through the UN80 integrated supply chain initiative. Food security and nutrition We stressed our commitment to food security and nutrition to address the consequences of conflicts and instability, and to strengthen food systems resilience. We called for continuing action to address the disruptions to food trade in the Black Sea in the context of the war in Ukraine, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the El Niño phenomenon. Together, in 2026, we mobilized 2.5 billion USD of international funding to address the crisis in the Middle East, adding to our long-term commitment to more resilient food systems and fertilizer markets. Forced displacement of people We noted the serious impact of conflict, violence, and instability on affected countries and regions, as well as on broader regional and international security affecting the security of civilian populations. This constitutes a driver of forced displacement and irregular migration, and exposes victims of human trafficking to acute forms of abuse and exploitation. Malicious hybrid activities We condemned persistent malicious hybrid activities by states and non-state actors aimed at undermining the security and stability of the G7 Members and partner countries, through coordinated and deliberate campaigns, including acts of sabotage against critical infrastructure, malicious cyber activities, foreign information manipulation and interference, and the instrumentalization of migration. Such actions risk unintended effects, escalation, and miscalculation. We reaffirmed our determination to act resolutely and in a coordinated manner to address hybrid campaigns, using all available tools to prevent, deter, and respond to these actions, irrespective of their origin, scale and intensity. We stressed the need to reinforce our common efforts and accelerate work on all relevant work strands, in order to strengthen resilience, enhance preparedness, and protect critical infrastructure. Transnational Organized Crime We expressed concern about the increasingly sophisticated methods, violence, and reach of transnational organized criminal groups worldwide, in particular those involved in drug trafficking, human trafficking, and migrant smuggling, and underscored the importance of international cooperation to strengthen maritime security, combat illicit trafficking networks, and dismantle these groups. We also recognized that online scams are a form of rapidly growing transnational organized crime that poses a threat to regional and international peace and security, and stressed the need to strengthen collaboration, including with the private sector, as appropriate, and to disrupt online scam networks, which may be linked to other forms of transnational organized crime. Maritime and port security We reaffirmed the absolute necessity of ensuring maritime safety and security, and of safeguarding freedom of navigation worldwide, in accordance with international law as reflected in the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), in order to prevent any lasting disruption to global supply chains, particularly with regard to energy, fertilizers and food products, because this can seriously affect vulnerable economies and populations. We recalled the global pledge initiated by the EU of 12 October 2026 on maintaining the integrity of the international law of the sea “No Fees, No Tolls”. We also underlined the need to strengthen the resilience and protection of critical undersea infrastructure, particularly submarine energy infrastructure and telecommunications cables, and their landing stations, including through enhanced international cooperation, information-sharing, redundancy and rapid repair capabilities. We encouraged practical cooperation with industry to improve access to repair vessels, equipment and spare parts, and to facilitate timely authorizations and port access for repairs, consistent with applicable international law and national requirements. In order to strengthen operational cooperation across our key maritime ports or relevant authorities, we, together with Brazil and the Republic of Korea, launched the G7+ Ports Network to Combat Drug Trafficking. This network will help strengthen operational cooperation, the exchange of information and the sharing of best practices to protect our ports from drug trafficking, in coordination and coherence with existing initiatives such as the European Ports Alliance, the European Coalition Against Drugs and the Maritime Safety Committee, and with the support of international organizations, in particular the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. We welcomed the work of the members of the G7++ “Friends of the Gulf of Guinea” group to create opportunities for deeper engagement with the Yaoundé Architecture for strengthening partnerships in the fields of training, capacity-building and joint operations, as well as our judicial cooperation to facilitate the prosecution of traffickers apprehended at sea. We welcomed the work carried out by the members of the G7 and Nordic Baltic 8++ Shadow Fleet Task Force and reiterated our commitment to enhance G7 coordination with partners to further disrupt and deter the global shadow fleet engaged in illegal, unsafe or environmentally perilous activities. Resilience of critical satellite infrastructure We also recognized the need to strengthen the resilience of critical satellite infrastructure, including satellites, ground stations and control centres, and their supporting terrestrial connections and power supplies. We encouraged stronger protection against physical and cyber threats and harmful interference, as well as redundancy and contingency arrangements to maintain essential services. Taking into account the interdependence of undersea, satellite and terrestrial networks, we encouraged cooperation among competent authorities and operators on risk assessment, timely and secure incident information-sharing, and preparedness exercises. Such cooperation should support rapid service restoration, including through complementary connectivity options for essential communications, while safeguarding sensitive information. Frontier models We recognized the opportunities offered by frontier models to advance science and strengthen our economies, while also noting the need to ensure the secure and trustworthy development of these advanced systems and models through adequate safeguards and human-centric adoption, taking into account that they can pose risks, including for society and economic security. We acknowledged that frontier models can be misused by state and non-state malicious actors, including for malicious cyber activities and criminal activities, or to acquire and enhance chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear or explosive capabilities. We recognized the importance of strengthening the security and resilience of frontier models to advance innovation, economic prosperity, and national security. The developments and issues are complex. That is why it is key that governments, international organizations businesses and academia engage in discussions on model adoption. We will pursue our discussion to advance a secure innovation ecosystem for trusted frontier model deployment including through efforts started with the Hiroshima AI Process. Economic security and critical minerals We reaffirmed our shared concerns regarding the use of non-market policies and practices and economic coercion, especially on critical minerals and their related dual-use items. We will work towards strengthening our competitiveness and addressing the root causes of our common challenges. We affirmed the importance of the G7 Coordination Platform on Economic Coercion to build a common response to economic coercion and further promote cooperation with partners beyond the G7. We further recognized the importance of maintaining and strengthening of our midstream and downstream industries’ competitiveness, including in relation to critical minerals, by protecting critical technologies and commit to working within the G7 and with partners to coordinate on policy measures for technology control. Recognizing the strategic role of critical minerals value chains for the economic prosperity and security of our countries, and in light of the high market concentration in certain economies in the critical minerals sector, we reiterated the urgency of reducing strategic dependencies and vulnerabilities by diversifying and securing trusted supply chains to build up our collective resilience. In that regard, we recognized the importance of the measures announced at the Evian Summit to ensure critical minerals supply chains resilience and security. We commended the expansion of the G7 Critical Minerals Resilience and Production Alliance which builds on the G7 Critical Minerals Production Alliance launched under Canada’s G7 Presidency in 2025. This expanded Alliance and other platforms provide a venue for cooperation within the G7 and with partner countries in order to facilitate discussion, support data-driven decision-making and foster coordination among members to strengthen diversification and resilience of critical minerals value chains. 黄仁勋退出英伟达对华盛顿、华尔街和北京意味着什么 - 大西洋理事会
东亚科技与创新美国和加拿大
黄仁勋退出英伟达对华盛顿、华尔街和北京意味着什么
有很多事情需要处理。周四，英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋因婚外情报道而辞职，其中包括与一名疑似中国间谍的婚外情。但其影响超出了该人和他的前公司的范围，该公司因其领先的计算机处理器而成为人工智能（AI）繁荣的关键引擎。下面，大西洋理事会专家将探讨人事变动将如何影响美国政策、全球市场等。
今天为您带来的专家反应
Trisha Ray：地质技术中心副主任兼常驻研究员
Graham Brookie (@GrahamBrookie)：技术项目和战略副总裁
Jessie Yin：地缘经济中心副主任
Kenton Thibaut (@kentonthibaut)：数字取证研究实验室中国高级研究员
Trisha 解释道，英伟达的先进芯片是“美国减缓对手人工智能能力的关键”。但这种优势也是“单点故障”，因为美国的出口管制力度取决于少数公司及其内部人员的安全措施。
格雷厄姆认为，这一事件并不是美国情报部门的失败，“而是美国政府在管理国家安全威胁方面协调和政策执行方面的更广泛的失败”。由于人工智能行业容易受到知识产权盗窃和直接攻击，华盛顿在风险管理和出口政策执行方面“措手不及”。
“对于投资者来说，将英伟达的成功与黄仁勋分开是很困难的，而对于华盛顿来说，将英伟达与国家安全分开也几乎同样困难，”杰西说。她现在认为国会有机会对该公司对国家安全的影响进行更大的监督，并加强半导体出口管制。肯顿指出，国会对芯片限制的势头不断增强，例如《人工智能监督法案》、《芯片安全法案》和《匹配法案》。
展望未来，特丽莎敦促政府加强审查。她认为，“鉴于支持美国人工智能领先地位的公司很少，政策制定者应该认真考虑政府的直接监督”，例如对公司领导层及其主要客户的安全许可要求，以及对出口实体的安全审计作为出口许可证的先决条件。
由于英伟达股价下跌，今天市场小幅下跌。黄仁勋的离开让投资者怀疑，如果没有这位已成为其成功代名词的领导者，英伟达能否维持其主导地位。杰西推测，公司“将在一段时间内不稳定”。
这些股份比英伟达的股价还要高。格雷厄姆警告说，美国经济已经高度依赖于少数人工智能公司的命运，这些公司“也恰好是该国在地缘政治竞争的决定性领域中的主要战略资产”。其中一个失败可能会影响整个美国经济和国家安全生态系统。
除了销售芯片之外，英伟达还成为人工智能热潮的主要融资者——被称为“人工智能中央银行”——投资初创企业并为购买其产品的客户提供支持。杰西表示，未来几个月将展示“英伟达对人工智能需求本身的整合程度如何”。

What Jensen Huang’s Nvidia exit means for Washington, Wall Street, and Beijing
It’s a lot to process. On Thursday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. But the implications extend beyond the man and his former company, a critical engine of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom because of its leading-edge computer processors. Below, Atlantic Council experts work through how the personnel shakeup could impact US policy, global markets, and more.
TODAY’S EXPERT REACTION BROUGHT TO YOU BY
Trisha Ray: Associate director and resident fellow at the GeoTech Center
Graham Brookie (@GrahamBrookie): Vice president for technology programs and strategy
Jessie Yin: Associate director with the GeoEconomics Center
Kenton Thibaut (@kentonthibaut): Senior resident China fellow at the Digital Forensic Research Lab
Nvidia’s advanced chips are “the linchpin of the United States’ leverage in slowing down the AI capabilities of its adversaries,” Trisha explains. But that advantage is also “a single point of failure,” since US export controls are only as strong as the security practices of a handful of companies and people within them.
Graham sees the incident not as a failure in US intelligence, “but rather a broader failure of coordination and policy execution in how the US government manages national security threats.” With the AI industry vulnerable to intellectual property theft and direct targeting, Washington was “caught flat footed” in risk management and export policy enforcement.
“As difficult as it is for investors to separate Nvidia’s success from Jensen Huang, it has become nearly as difficult for Washington to separate Nvidia from national security,” Jessie argues. She now sees an opening for Congress to exert greater oversight of the company’s impact on national security and tighten semiconductor export controls. Kenton points to growing momentum in Congress behind chip restrictions such as the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, and the MATCH Act.
Going forward, Trisha urges greater government scrutiny. “Given how few companies underpin the US AI lead, policymakers should seriously consider direct government oversight,” she argues, such as security clearance–like requirements for company leadership and their major customers, as well as security audits of the exporting entities as a precondition for export licenses.
Markets were down slightly today, as Nvidia shares took a hit. Huang’s departure has investors wondering if Nvidia can sustain its dominance without the leader who became a synonym to its success. The company is “going to be unsteady for a while,” Jessie surmises.
The stakes are higher than Nvidia’s stock price alone. The US economy is already highly exposed to the fortunes of a handful of AI companies that “also happen to be the country’s primary strategic assets in a determinative domain of geopolitical competition,” Graham warns. A failure at one could reverberate across the US economy and national security ecosystem.
Beyond selling chips, Nvidia has become a major financier of the AI boom—known as “the central bank of AI”—investing in startups and supporting customers that buy its products. Jessie says that the coming months will show “how integral Nvidia has become to AI demand itself.”

Ahead of a planned meeting next week between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Beijing warned Washington earlier today against further technology restrictions, Kenton notes.
Huang had long opposed strict export controls and was able to speak with both Trump and Xi. “But with Huang out of the picture, there is potentially more political leeway to push forward on a more hawkish approach,” Kenton says.
Jessie adds that the scandal has “permanently damaged the company’s credibility to push back on export controls,” relationships aside.
But tougher controls could invite retaliation, Kenton warns. “Beijing could answer new restrictions with curbs on critical minerals or probes of other American firms,” potentially complicating the upcoming Trump-Xi meeting.

content:
来自四个国家的七枚火箭将于本周发射。星际飞船将尝试其迄今为止最重要的任务，而猎鹰 9 号将为美国太空军发射一对机密有效载荷。联合发射联盟计划让 Vulcan 执行其返回飞行任务，而 Electron 则将完成具有里程碑意义的第 100 次任务。在国际上，中国和韩国将分别发射未知的有效载荷和演示任务。猎鹰 9 号 | USSF-627（“R-5”）本周首次发射将由猎鹰 9 号火箭为美国太空军 (USSF) 提供机密有效载荷。该任务被指定为 USSF-627，最初计划于 11 月 8 日星期日发射。猎鹰 9 号现定于太平洋标准时间 11 月 9 日星期一晚上 7:07（世界标准时间 10 月 10 日 03:07）从范登堡太空部队基地 (VSFB) 的 4 号东部太空发射综合体 (SLC-4E) 起飞，距太平洋标准时间晚上 11:03 (07:03) 的窗口期已过去四分钟。 UTC 时间 11 月 10 日）。由于有效载荷的机密性质，卫星的确切数量尚不清楚。一些迹象表明，基于猎鹰 9 号第二级的降落区，星盾将进行发射。 Starshield是为美国政府打造的Starlink版本，其主要客户是USSF、国家侦察办公室和太空发展局。范登堡太空部队基地 4E 号航天发射场发射台上的猎鹰 9 号火箭。
（图片来源：SpaceX） Falcon 9 是一款两级、70 m 高、部分可重复使用的火箭，第一级使用九个 Merlin 1D 海平面发动机，第二级使用单个真空优化的 Merlin 1D。Falcon 9 的第一级着陆在自主无人机船上或着陆点，其整流罩在飞行后回收并重复使用。两个阶段都使用液体煤油和液氧作为推进剂。助推器 B1103 将在其第七次飞行中支持这项任务。此前，该助推器已支持 NROL-179、第一批传输层 A 和 E 以及三个星链任务的发射。猎鹰 9 号将搭乘 SpaceX 的无人机“当然我仍然爱你”着陆。米尔 |演示飞行 11 月 10 日星期二，韩国计划发射韩国军方小型卫星运载火箭和平号的第二次飞行。继 2023 年 12 月进行了不包括第二级的试飞之后，此次发射将是全尺寸火箭的首次轨道飞行。启动窗口于 05:00 UTC 开始，并延长至 09:00 UTC。和平号是一款四级固体燃料运载火箭，第四级采用液体燃料，可实现精确入轨。 2023 年 12 月飞行的版本能够运载 700 公斤至近地轨道，该版本疑似能够运载 1,000 公斤左右。长征2D |有效载荷未知 11 月 11 日星期三，长征 2D (CZ-2D) 火箭计划从酒泉卫星发射中心发射升空。
目前，发射计划于 11:40 UTC 进行，距离 11:32 UTC 开启并持续到 12:05 UTC 的窗口还有 8 分钟的时间。CZ-2D 将向轨道发射未知有效载荷。 CZ-2D 是一款两级、41 米高的运载火箭，能够向近地轨道 (LEO) 发射 3,500 公斤的重量。 CZ-2D的第一级和第二级均由四氧化二氮和不对称二甲肼提供动力，这两种推进剂都是自燃推进剂。周三的发射将是长征二号丁的第 107 次发射，也是 2026 年的第六次发射。快舟 11 |有效载荷未知本周第二个也是最后一个预定的中国任务

【原文 English Original】
Seven rockets from four countries are set to launch this week. Starship is set to attempt its most consequential mission yet, while Falcon 9 is set to launch a pair of classified payloads for the United States Space Force. The United Launch Alliance is scheduled to fly Vulcan on its return-to-flight mission, and Electron is set to reach a milestone 100th mission. Internationally, China and South Korea are set to launch an unknown payload and a demonstration mission, respectively. Falcon 9 | USSF-627 (“R-5”) The first launch of the week will feature Falcon 9 delivering a classified payload for the United States Space Force (USSF). The mission, designated USSF-627, was initially scheduled to launch on Sunday, Nov. 8. Falcon 9 is now set to take off from Space Launch Complex 4 East (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) on Monday, Nov. 9, at 7:07 PM PST (03:07 UTC on Nov. 10), four minutes into a window that extends until 11:03 PM PST (07:03 UTC on Nov. 10). Due to the classified nature of the payload, the exact quantity of satellites is unknown. Some indicators suggest a Starshield launch, based on drop zones for Falcon 9’s second stage. Starshield is a version of Starlink built for the United States government, with its primary customers being the USSF, National Reconnaissance Office, and the Space Development Agency. A Falcon 9 on the launch pad at Space Launch Complex-4E on Vandenberg Space Force Base. (Credit: SpaceX) Falcon 9 is a two-stage, 70 m-tall, partially reusable rocket that uses nine Merlin 1D sea-level engines on its first stage and a single vacuum-optimized Merlin 1D on its second stage. Falcon 9’s first stage lands either aboard an autonomous droneship or at a landing site, with its fairings being recovered and reused after flight. Both stages utilize liquid kerosene and liquid oxygen as propellants. Booster B1103 will be supporting this mission on its seventh flight. Previously, this booster has supported the launches of NROL-179, Tranche 1 Transport Layers A and E, and three Starlink missions. Falcon 9 will land downrange aboard SpaceX’s droneship Of Course I Still Love You . Mir | Demo Flight On Tuesday, Nov. 10, South Korea is set to launch the second flight of Mir, the South Korean military’s small satellite launch vehicle. This launch is set to be the first orbital flight of the full-scale rocket, following a test flight in December 2023 that did not include the second stage. The launch window opens at 05:00 UTC and extends until 09:00 UTC. Mir is a four-stage, solid-fuel launch vehicle with a liquid-fueled fourth stage for precise orbital insertion. The version that flew in December 2023 was capable of 700 kg to LEO, with this version suspected to be capable of around 1,000 kg. Chang Zheng 2D | Unknown Payload On Wednesday, Nov. 11, a Chang Zheng 2D (CZ-2D) rocket is scheduled to launch out of the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center. The launch is currently scheduled for 11:40 UTC, eight minutes into a window that opens at 11:32 UTC and extends until 12:05 UTC. CZ-2D will deliver an unknown payload into orbit. CZ-2D is a two-stage, 41 m-tall launch vehicle capable of delivering 3,500 kg to low-Earth orbit (LEO). CZ-2D’s first and second stages are both powered by dinitrogen tetroxide and unsymmetrical dimethyl hydrazine, both hypergolic propellants. Wednesday’s launch will be the 107th overall for CZ-2D, and sixth in 2026. Kuaizhou 11 | Unknown Payload The second and final scheduled Chinese mission of the week will see a Kuaizhou 11 rocket launch on Thursday, Nov. 12. Liftoff is set for 19:50 UTC from Site 95A at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, during a 45-minute launch window. Kuaizhou 11 is a four-stage Chinese rocket manufactured by the China Aerospace Science and Industry Corporation. Standing 25.3 m tall, the rocket can loft 1,500 kg to LEO with a liftoff thrust of 1,250 kN. This mission will be the eighth overall Kuaizhou 11 mission and the fourth of 2026. Vulcan VC6L | Amazon Leo (LV-01) United Launch Alliance’s (ULA) Vulcan rocket is set to launch on Friday, Nov. 13, from Space Launch Complex 41 (SLC-41) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. The 30-minute launch window opens at 12:54 PM EST (17:54 UTC). This will be the first flight of Vulcan in over nine months, following the ejection of one of Vulcan’s GEM-63XL solid rocket boosters at T+69 seconds on the USSF-87 mission. Flying aboard Vulcan will be a stack of 40 Amazon Leo satellites for Amazon’s Leo satellite internet constellation, a rival to SpaceX’s Starlink. A ULA Vulcan (USSF-87) sits next to a SpaceX Crew Dragon (Crew-12). (Credit: Tyler Gray for NSF) Vulcan is a two-stage launch vehicle with a range of launch configurations. Vulcan’s first stage is powered by two BE-4 engines built by Blue Origin, running on liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants. Its second stage, Centaur V, is powered by twin RL10C engines running on liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. Centaur V can be configured as Centaur LEO, High Energy, or Endurance. Vulcan can also be configured with solid rocket boosters to augment liftoff thrust, with options ranging from zero to two, four, or six boosters. The payload is encapsulated by either a short (15.5 m) or a long (21.3 m) fairing. Vulcan will debut the Vulcan VC6L variant, designated by six solid boosters and the long fairing option. Vulcan will debut the LEO-optimized Centaur V, which is 1.94 m smaller than the existing Centaur V High Energy, which has flown on all previous Vulcan launches. Additionally, this flight is a certification flight of this Vulcan configuration for the United States Space Force. Amazon Leo (LV-01) will be the first of 38 scheduled for Vulcan and the fifth overall mission for Vulcan. Starship | Flight 15 / Starlink Group 31-2 Pending regulatory approval, Starship is set to fly its next, and most significant, mission no earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, at 4:45 PM CST (22:45 UTC). The launch window extends until 6:00 PM CST (00:00 UTC on Nov. 14). Flight 15 will feature two notable events: the first booster-catch attempt since Flight 8, following stage separation, and the first attempt to catch the ship, roughly 22 hours after liftoff. Starship is a two-stage, super-heavy-lift launch vehicle capable of lofting an estimated 100 tonnes. The first stage, named Super Heavy, features 33 Raptor 3 engines, running off of liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants. The second stage, named Starship, features six Raptor 3 engines, three sea-level and three vacuum-optimized, also running off of liquid methane and liquid oxygen. Flying on Flight 15 will be Ship 42 and Booster 22, both on their first flights. Flight 15 is expected to deliver 26 Starlink v3 satellites to LEO. Like Flight 14, three of these satellites will feature imaging capabilities for imaging the heat shield of Starship in orbit. Flight 15 will be the 15th full-stack launch of Starship and the fourth for the system’s V3 configuration. Falcon 9 | USSF-317 (“R-6”) Falcon 9 is set to fly again on Friday, Nov. 13, from VSFB with another USSF mission. The designation for this flight is USSF-317. The launch window opens at 8:09 PM PST (04:09 UTC on Nov. 14), and lasts for four hours. This mission will fly another unknown quantity of presumed Starshield satellites to LEO. Booster B1100 will support this mission, marking its 11th flight. This booster has previously supported NROL-105, USSF-385, and eight Starlink missions. B1100 will land downrange aboard SpaceX’s droneship Of Course I Still Love You . Electron during its 95th launch “Happily Ever Faster.” Credit: Rocket Lab) Electron | The Mountain God Rises The last scheduled launch of the week will see Rocket Lab’s Electron launch from the Mahia Peninsula in New Zealand on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 05:30 UTC. This flight of Electron, named “The Mountain God Rises,” will deliver another iQPS satellite into LEO for iQPS’s synthetic aperture radar constellation (SAR). SAR is used to image the surface of the Earth and can penetrate through cloud layers. Electron is a two-stage small-lift vehicle capable of delivering up to 300 kg to LEO and 200 kg to Sun-synchronous orbit. The vehicle is fueled by liquid kerosene and liquid oxygen, which powers nine Rutherford engines on the first stage and a single vacuum-optimized Rutherford on the second stage. This mission will serve as Electron’s 100th overall mission — a notable milestone for the small rocket that first flew in 2017. In addition, this mission will serve as the 269th orbital launch attempt worldwide in 2026. ( Lead Image: Falcon 9 launches from Florida. Credit: Julia Bergeron for NSF) The post Launch Preview: Starship, Vulcan, and Electron launches scheduled for busy week appeared first on NASASpaceFlight.com .

台湾本土农民复兴气候适应型小米 - 日本时报
台湾本土农民复兴气候适应型小米
10 月 21 日，农民林卡夫·伊斯马哈桑（左）和巴努·伊斯马哈桑在台湾台东的一块田里收割油小米。60 多年前，随着稻米变得更加容易获得，油小米曾是台湾原住民农民为了防止主要农作物枯死而种植的油小米，基本上从田地里消失了。 |法新社-即时
X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads 电子邮件 打印 书签故事 复制链接
台湾——土著农民巴努·伊斯玛哈桑 (Banu Ismahasan) 走过台湾东南部一片长满高秆的金色田野，用手收割一种能抵抗极端天气的古老作物的谷粒。
60 多年前，随着稻米变得更加容易获得，油小米曾由台湾原住民农民种植，以防主粮枯死。
在过去的十年里，伊斯马哈桑和他年迈的父母一直在台东县布克拉武村的布农社区努力恢复几乎被遗忘的农作物。
“我们只是希望带回许多传统的布农族作物，并在这片土地上重新种植它们，”48 岁的伊斯马哈桑在晴朗的蓝天下的油小米田里说道。
油小米，或布农语中的莳萝，是台湾特有的植物，可以在山上野生生长。
伊斯玛哈桑首先在网上了解到这种植物，然后开始自己的研究，梳理历史文献并与部落长老交谈，其中包括一位记得上次吃这种植物是在半个世纪前的妇女。
他发现，布农族农民过去常常在种植主要作物谷子的同时种植油小米，作为收成歉收或发生灾害时的“后备”。
经过多年亲自种植油小米，伊斯玛哈桑开始明白为什么他的祖先依赖这种作物。
一粒油小米种子可以长出 15 至 20 个圆锥花序，或分枝种子簇，并且茎可以自行再生，而谷子通常每粒种子长出一个圆锥花序，必须在割下后重新播种。
当极端天气或疾病爆发蹂躏他 2.2 公顷 5.4 英亩的农场时，事实证明，它比谷子更顽强。
伊斯马哈桑说，几年前一场持续了 200 多天的干旱期间，油小米“保持鲜绿色”，而其他作物却枯萎了。
台风、洪水，甚至锈病爆发也没有影响到它。
台湾中央研究院退休教授、植物遗传学专家邢月娥15年前在一个国际论坛上第一次听说了油小米。
幸不知道的是，1890 年代采集的台湾油粟标本就存放在英国皇家植物园 (Kew)。
兴带领一个研究小组在台湾东南部的山区找到了油小米，并开始研究这种鲜为人知的谷物。
10 月 21 日，台湾台东，农民巴努·伊斯马哈桑 (Banu Ismahasan) 将刚收获的油小米摊开在阳光下晒干。法新社-即时
她发现，种子的保护性蜡涂层使其无需灌溉、化肥或杀虫剂即可生长，即使在质量较差的土地上也是如此。
它富含油、蛋白质和矿物质，可供人类和动物食用，也可用作燃料。
“它在利用阳光和水方面自然非常有效，”辛说。
“至于土壤条件，即使是在地面布满大石头的山区，它也能生长得很好。”
伊斯玛哈桑从一粒油小米开始了他的收成。家里现在收割了两次油小米

Taiwan Indigenous farmer revives climate-resilient millet
Farmers Linkav Ismahasan (left) and Banu Ismahasan harvest oil millet in a field in Taitung, Taiwan, on Oct. 21. Once grown by Indigenous farmers in Taiwan in case their staple crops died, oil millet largely disappeared from fields more than 60 years ago as rice became more available. | AFP-JIJI
X Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Bluesky Threads Email Print Bookmark story Copy link
Taiwan – Indigenous farmer Banu Ismahasan walks through a golden field of tall stalks in southeastern Taiwan, harvesting by hand the grain heads of an ancient crop resistant to extreme weather.
Once grown by Indigenous farmers in Taiwan in case their staple crops died, oil millet largely disappeared from fields more than 60 years ago as rice became more available.
Over the past decade, Ismahasan and his elderly parents have worked to revive the nearly forgotten crop in the Bunun community in Buklavu, a village surrounded by lush green mountains in Taitung county.
“We just hope to bring back many traditional Bunun crops and grow them on this land again,” Ismahasan, 48, said in his oil millet field under a clear blue sky.
Oil millet, or dill in the Bunun language, is endemic to Taiwan and can be found growing wild in the mountains.
Ismahasan first read about the plant online and then embarked on his own research, combing through historical documents and speaking to tribal elders, including a woman who recalled last eating it half a century ago.
He discovered that Bunun farmers used to grow oil millet alongside their staple crop foxtail millet as a “back-up” when harvests failed or disasters hit.
After years of growing oil millet himself, Ismahasan came to understand why his ancestors relied on the crop.
A single oil millet seed can grow 15 to 20 panicles, or branching seed clusters, and the stems regenerate on their own, while foxtail millet typically grows one panicle per seed and must be sown again after being cut.
It has also proven hardier than foxtail millet when extreme weather or disease outbreaks have ravaged his 2.2-hectare 5.4-acre farm.
During a drought several years ago that lasted more than 200 days, the oil millet “stayed bright green” while other crops withered, Ismahasan said.
Typhoons, floods and even a rust disease outbreak have not affected it either.
Hsing Yue-ie, a retired professor from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica and an expert in plant genetics, first heard of oil millet 15 years ago at an international forum.
Unbeknownst to Hsing, specimens of Taiwan oil millet collected in the 1890s were sitting in Britain’s Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew.
Hsing led a research team to find oil millet in the mountains of southeastern Taiwan and began studying the little-known cereal.
Farmer Banu Ismahasan spreads freshly harvested oil millet out to dry in the sun in Taitung, Taiwan, on Oct. 21. | AFP-JIJI
She found that the seed’s protective wax coating enabled it to grow without irrigation, fertilizers or pesticides, even on poor-quality land.
Rich in oil, protein and minerals, it can be used for human and animal consumption, as well as for fuel.
“It’s naturally very efficient at using sunlight and water,” said Hsing.
“As for soil conditions, even in mountainous areas where the ground is full of large rocks, it can still grow very well.”
Ismahasan started his crop with one panicle of oil millet. The family now harvests oil millet twice a year on a section of their property where they grow other traditional Bunun cereal crops.
Tiny and tasteless, oil millet can be used in porridge, steamed buns, bread and even popcorn.
But the family has struggled to convince other farmers to grow it because it is not yet commercially viable.
Oil millet is not only labor intensive but also significantly more expensive for consumers than rice, by far Taiwan’s most popular staple.
While the current market for oil millet is limited, Taiwan’s National Crop Germplasm Center sees value in preserving its seeds for the future, when climate change might force more farmers to consider growing the crop.
Oil millet seeds are “very precious” because of their genetic diversity and ability to adapt to the environment, said Lin Yen-yu, an assistant researcher at the center.
Seeds are kept in aluminum foil packets and stored at minus 18 degrees Celsius under low-moisture conditions where they can last for decades, Lin said.
“In the future, when cultivation methods or climate change undergo certain shifts, their value may start to be recognized and discovered,” he said. “It preserves many possibilities.”
Ismahasan said his priority for now was to get more people in his community growing and eating oil millet, bringing “it back into our everyday lives, just as it was for our elders.”
“If we don’t even eat it ourselves anymore, how can we expect to turn it into a viable business?” he said.

2026 年 11 月 13 日

日本横须贺——

由军事海运司令部运营的远征快速运输舰俾斯麦市号（EPF 9）迎来了新任指挥官，中校。蒂亚·迈尔斯在横须贺舰队活动船上举行的仪式上。迈尔斯从中校手中接过指挥权。 VanAnh McCormick，在将该船移交给 MILCREW II 之前担任军事船员 I 的指挥官。

“从我们的人员流动开始，我们不再是 MILCREW II 和 CIVMAR；我们都是俾斯麦市号航空母舰，”迈尔斯在向由水手和公务员组成的混合船员发表的讲话中说道。 “‘保持媒体报道’是我们的全部工作！我们必须在场并准备好参与，同时互相支持，以确保我们的成功。Crew I 奠定了基础，我们的工作就是在此基础上继续发展。Possumus Efficiemus：我们可以而且我们将会实现。”

迈尔斯是南卡罗来纳州哥伦比亚人，2014 年从弗朗西斯马里恩大学毕业并获得数学学士学位后，被任命为海军军官。她还拥有海军研究生院的高级工商管理硕士学位。

在海上，迈尔斯曾在阿利伯克号航空母舰 (DDG 51)、珍珠港号航空母舰 (LSD 52) 和哈珀斯渡口号航空母舰 (LSD 49) 上服役。
在岸上，她在圣地亚哥海军水面和水雷作战发展中心和水面高级作战学校担任两栖作战战术教员。迈尔斯接替了麦考密克，麦考密克于 2026 年 7 月接管了 MILCREW I 的指挥权，并带领船员完成了有史以来的首次 EPF 部署。部署期间，船员航行超过4000海里，访问了4个海外港口。机组人员为“锐剑”演习提供了后勤保障，并完成了任务要求的所有准备工作。此外，供应部门还入围了 David M. Cook 食品服务卓越奖的决赛。

俾斯麦号是EPF级第九艘舰艇。这些浅吃水、全铝制商用双体船旨在以 35 节的平均速度将 600 短吨军用货物运输 1,200 海里。该船设有用于直升机操作的飞行甲板、车辆卸载坡道部署以及增强沿海操作和港口通道的浅吃水。这些能力使 EPF 能够在严峻或受损的港口提供灵活的物流支持、快速运输和救灾。

该船的船员由军事人员和文职海员组成。 MILCREW 轮流部署，基地设在圣地亚哥，而该舰的母港是横须贺，由美国第七舰队负责作战控制。
军事海运司令部负责指挥和支持大约 140 艘民用船只的行动，这些船只为美国海军舰船补充海上补给、执行专门任务、在全球范围内预置战斗货物、提供支持服务以及向部署的美国部队运输军事装备和补给品。

13 November 2026

YOKOSUKA, Japan --

The expeditionary fast transport USS City of Bismarck (EPF 9), operated by Military Sealift Command, welcomed its new commanding officer, Lt. Cmdr. Tia Myers, during a ceremony aboard the ship at Fleet Activities Yokosuka. Myers assumed command from Lt. Cmdr. VanAnh McCormick, who served as the Military Crew I commander before turning the ship over to MILCREW II.

“Starting with our turnover, we are no longer MILCREW II and CIVMARs; we are all USS City of Bismarck,” Myers said in her address to the hybrid crew of sailors and civil service mariners. “It is all of our job to ‘keep the press!’ We have to be present and ready to engage while supporting each other to ensure our success. Crew I laid the foundation, and it is our job to build upon it. Possumus Efficiemus: We can and we will accomplish.”

A native of Columbia, South Carolina, Myers commissioned as a naval officer in 2014 after graduating from Francis Marion University with a bachelor’s degree in mathematics. She also holds an executive master’s degree in business administration from the Naval Postgraduate School.

At sea, Myers served aboard USS Arleigh Burke (DDG 51), USS Pearl Harbor (LSD 52) and USS Harpers Ferry (LSD 49).

Ashore, she served as an amphibious warfare tactics instructor at the Naval Surface and Mine Warfighting Development Center and Surface Advanced Warfighting School in San Diego. Myers relieved McCormick, who took command of MILCREW I in July 2026 and led the crew through its first ever EPF deployment. During the deployment, the crew sailed more than 4,000 nautical miles and visited four overseas ports. The crew provided logistics support for Exercise Keen Sword and completed all ready for tasking requirements. In addition, the supply department became a finalist for the David M. Cook Food Service Excellence Award.

Bismarck is the ninth ship in the EPF class. These shallow-draft, all-aluminum, commercial-based catamarans are designed to transport 600 short tons of military cargo 1,200 nautical miles at an average speed of 35 knots. The ship features a flight deck for helicopter operations, a vehicle offload ramp deployment, and a shallow draft that enhances littoral operations and port access. These capabilities allow the EPF to deliver flexible logistics support, rapid transport and disaster relief in austere or damaged ports.

The ship operates with a hybrid crew of military personnel and civil service mariners. The MILCREWs rotate for deployments and are based in San Diego, while the ship is homeported in Yokosuka under the operational control of U.S. 7th Fleet.

Military Sealift Command directs and supports operations for approximately 140 civilian-crewed ships that replenish U.S. Navy ships at sea, conduct specialized missions, preposition combat cargo worldwide, provide support services, and transport military equipment and supplies to deployed U.S. forces.
